paragraphs.text: *A specialist account of the PCP proof of Amireddy, Behera, Srinivasan, Sudan and Willumsgaard, following Troy Lee's formalization*
paragraphs.purpose: Identify the source proof and formalization.
paragraphs.attention: The paragraph gives a needed definition, hypothesis, inference or qualification directly. Standard terminology, meaningful contrasts and all mathematical content remain.

paragraphs.text: The PCP theorem states that every language in NP has a polynomial-time verifier with logarithmic randomness, constantly many proof-bit queries, perfect completeness and constant soundness error. The algebraic proof of Amireddy, Behera, Srinivasan, Sudan and Willumsgaard obtains these resources by encoding line polynomials as constant-degree multivariate polynomials and encoding field values by low-degree Hadamard words. This permits a point-versus-line test and a correction procedure to operate through constantly many bits. We explain the resulting construction for three-colourability, including the Lagrange-weighted test in the corrected paper, correction at the nonuniform points used by vanishing certificates, and the common decoding argument that makes the seven verifier checks sound. The quantitative statements follow Lee's formal implementation; its sampling conventions and query counts differ in several places from the paper. The contribution of this account is an explanatory reconstruction of that proof.
paragraphs.purpose: State the PCP resources, encoding mechanism, scope and source conventions.

paragraphs.text: Arora–Safra and Arora–Lund–Motwani–Sudan–Szegedy established the PCP characterization in their foundational work [2,3]. Our subject is the algebraic proof in the corrected version of [1], as implemented by Lee [5]. Its central problem is already visible in the usual point-versus-line test. Reading a field value costs several bits; reading a line polynomial by its coefficient vector costs its degree times as many. Treating either object as one oracle symbol does not prove constant **bit** query complexity.
paragraphs.purpose: Place the constant-query theorem historically and identify the alphabet-cost problem.
paragraphs.attention: ALMSS proves constant queries; Arora–Safra is its precursor. Use the actual abstract attribution and name the field-value versus bit-query cost directly.

paragraphs.text: The construction resolves these costs by two encodings. A base-$b$ digit expansion turns a degree-$O(b^c)$ line polynomial into a degree-$c$ polynomial in $cb$ variables. Here $c$ is fixed while $b$ grows. A Hadamard word then makes a binary observation of a field value accessible in one query. The encoded line is tested and locally corrected, so its value at the required digit-substitution point can be recovered despite errors. This supplies the local operations needed to verify polynomial constraints directly. An auxiliary line oracle remains part of the proof, but the verifier's acceptance computation is not recursively re-encoded through repeated PCP composition.
paragraphs.purpose: Explain how the two encodings avoid recursively encoding acceptance computations.
paragraphs.attention: Replace the vague action “supplies local operations” with the specific polynomial-constraint verification; keep the precise composition distinction.

paragraphs.text: For the converse, guess the first $p(n)$ proof bits and simulate the verifier on every random string. There are at most $2^b(2(n+2))^a$ such strings, and each simulation takes polynomial time. Perfect completeness gives a prefix for which every run accepts. If a prefix were accepted for a no-instance, its zero extension would be a fixed proof with acceptance probability one, contradicting soundness. Thus this finite witness relation is an NP relation, completing the equality in the theorem.
